benefits: Gives security researchers a standard way to contact you — no more guessing which email to use.
Follows RFC 9116, so automated scanners and bug-bounty platforms recognize it instantly.
Expires dates keep the file fresh: researchers know the contact info is current.
Preferred-Languages tells reporters which languages you actually read.
Generated locally; your contact details never leave the browser.

faqs.a: At https://yourdomain.com/.well-known/security.txt — the well-known URI defined by RFC 9116. Serve it as plain text over HTTPS. Researchers and scanners look there first.

At least one Contact line is required by RFC 9116 — without it the file is pointless. Expires is also required by the spec. Everything else (Encryption, Acknowledgments, Policy, Hiring, Canonical, Preferred-Languages) is optional.
Set it no more than a year in the future (the RFC recommends at most one year). When it passes, researchers should treat the file as stale. Renew it yearly — put a reminder in your calendar.
faqs.q: How far in the future should Expires be?

faqs.a: No. security.txt only advertises how to contact you about vulnerabilities. It doesn't scan, fix, or protect anything by itself. Pair it with an actual vulnerability disclosure policy page.
faqs.q: Does security.txt make my site more secure?

faqs.a: The Encryption field points to your PGP key so researchers can encrypt sensitive reports. You can link an https:// URL to the key file, or use an openpgp4fpr: fingerprint URI. Without it, reports arrive in plain email.
faqs.q: What is the Encryption field for?

faqs.a: If you serve security.txt from multiple locations or CDNs, Canonical declares the authoritative URL. It prevents confusion about which copy is current. Most small sites can skip it.
faqs.q: What is the Canonical field for?

security-txt-generator.formula:
security.txt field syntax (RFC 9116):
Contact: mailto:security@example.com     <- required, at least one
Expires: 2026-12-31T23:59:59Z            <- required, RFC 3339 timestamp
Encryption: https://example.com/key.txt  <- optional
Acknowledgments: https://...             <- optional
Policy: https://...                      <- optional
Hiring: https://...                      <- optional
Canonical: https://.../.well-known/security.txt  <- optional
Preferred-Languages: en, hi              <- optional
howTo: Enter at least one contact: an email address, an https:// contact URL, or a tel: link — one per line.
Pick an expiry date within the next year (required by the standard).
Optionally add your PGP key URL, acknowledgments page, disclosure policy, hiring page, and canonical URL.
List the languages you read, comma separated (for example: en, hi).
Copy or download security.txt and publish it at https://yourdomain.com/.well-known/security.txt.
keyFacts: security.txt is defined by RFC 9116: a standard file that tells security researchers how to report vulnerabilities.
It lives at the well-known URI /.well-known/security.txt on your domain, served over HTTPS.
Contact and Expires are the two required fields; everything else is optional.
Contact values can be mailto: emails, https:// URLs, or tel: links — this tool formats emails automatically.
Expires must be an RFC 3339 timestamp and should be at most one year in the future.
The file is advisory only — it advertises contact info, it does not secure anything by itself.

labels.contactsHint: One per line: email, https:// URL, or tel: link…
labels.expiresHint: Required. Rendered as end-of-day UTC in RFC 3339 format.
labels.languagesHint: Comma separated language codes, e.g. en, hi.
labels.publishNote: Serve this file over HTTPS at /.well-known/security.txt on your domain.
labels.warnExpiresInvalid: The expiry date is not a valid calendar date.
labels.warnExpiresPast: The expiry date is in the past — researchers will treat the file as stale.
labels.warnInvalidContact: Some contact lines were skipped because they are not a valid email, URL, or tel: link.
labels.warnInvalidUrl: One or more optional URLs are invalid (use full https:// URLs) and were left out.
labels.warnNoContact: At least one valid Contact is required — the file is currently empty.

limitations: Advisory only — it does not scan, fix, or prevent vulnerabilities.
Researchers may ignore it; publishing the file doesn't guarantee responsible disclosure.
Expires must be renewed (at most yearly) or the file is treated as stale.
This tool builds the file; serving it over HTTPS at the right path is up to you.

security-txt-generator.quickAnswer: A security.txt file (RFC 9116) published at yourdomain.com/.well-known/security.txt tells security researchers how to report vulnerabilities: who to contact, until when the info is valid, and optionally your PGP key, disclosure policy, and preferred languages. At minimum it needs Contact: mailto:security@example.com and an Expires: timestamp. This generator builds the file from a simple form and validates every field.

Inputs: contact security@example.com, expiry 2026-12-31, encryption key https://example.com/pgp-key.txt, policy https://example.com/security-policy, languages en, hi.
Generated file:
Contact: mailto:security@example.com
Expires: 2026-12-31T23:59:59Z
Encryption: https://example.com/pgp-key.txt
Policy: https://example.com/security-policy
Preferred-Languages: en, hi
Publish this at https://example.com/.well-known/security.txt over HTTPS. The expiry (end of 2026) is within the one-year recommended maximum.
